title: AI’s Historical Present: Did You Get This from AI?
author: Dawn Zimmerer
source: Nick Potkalitsky, AI's Historical Present (nickpotkalitsky.substack.com), October 26, 2026
summary: In this guest post for Nick Potkalitsky's series, community college librarian Dawn Zimmerer recalls the fall of 2023 when a faculty member brought her a student citation that could not be found. She and the instructor searched the journal, volume and author before realising the source was an AI hallucination presented as real. Fake citations soon arrived from faculty, chat reference and students at the desk, and a new question entered the reference interview: did you get this from AI? She describes how students, at a Primarily Black Institution used to being presumed guilty, hesitated out of fear, which led her to reword the question as a shared problem to solve. Over time her belief shifted from suspecting students of cheating to seeing shortcuts as natural. She concludes that educators must make the case for better methods without leading with suspicion.
points: Her first instinct on seeing a fake citation was to suspect the student, showing how professional habits can lag behind knowledge of AI hallucination.
A fabricated reference can look entirely real, with a genuine journal, plausible pages and a believable author.
Reframing the question as helping to fix the citation rather than policing it earned student trust at the reference desk.
Context matters because students at her institution are used to being presumed to be doing something wrong.
She now sees students as using the tools in front of them, which places the burden on educators to persuade rather than accuse.
quotes: I already knew about hallucinations. I’d been reading about ChatGPT for months, and I knew these tools could produce citations that looked real and weren’t.
When we finally do, the whole thing rearranges itself: a real journal, plausible page numbers, a believable author, and an article that never existed. It isn’t a typo.
A new question entered our reference interview that year, one that didn’t exist in 2022: Did you get this from AI?
When I asked students, the hesitation before they answered looked like fear. They didn’t know what kind of response they were going to get.
Our students get judged a lot just for existing. They walk into plenty of rooms where they’re already presumed to be doing something wrong.
The reason I’m asking is that AI has a tendency to make things up and hallucinate citations. I don’t want you to get dinged for a bad citation.
What I think now is that students use the tools in front of them, and they take shortcuts because the shortcuts are there. Most of us do.
It’s our job to convince them that the shortcut isn’t always the best way, and we can’t make that case if the first thing they hear from us sounds like suspicion.
